```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Panel count data, such as crashes on the same road segments over several
years, contain differences between units that the regressors do not
capture: driver populations, geometry, enforcement. Random-effects models
(`renb()`, `repois()`, `countreg_rp()` with a random intercept) treat these
differences as draws from a distribution that is independent of the
regressors. When that is doubtful (busier roads may also be different roads)
a **fixed-effects** model gives each unit its own intercept, so the slopes
are estimated only from changes *within* units.

`countreg_fe()` estimates fixed-effects count models. This article shows
when to use it, what it can and cannot estimate, and how its results
compare with pooled and random-effects models.

```{r setup}
library(flexCountReg)
data("washington_roads")
```

## 1. The model

For unit $i$ (here a road segment) in period $t$,

$$
E[y_{it} \mid x_{it}, \alpha_i] = \exp(\alpha_i + x_{it}'\beta + o_{it}),
$$

with a fixed effect $\alpha_i$ for each unit and an optional offset
$o_{it}$. Nothing is assumed about how $\alpha_i$ relates to $x_{it}$.

`countreg_fe()` chooses the estimator from the family and the number of
fixed-effect dimensions:

| Family | Fixed effects | Method | Notes |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Poisson | one (`~ site`) | conditional likelihood | the effects are conditioned out; consistent for fixed T with only a correct mean (Wooldridge 1999) |
| Poisson | several (`~ site + year`) | IRLS with alternating projections | the method of `fixest::fepois()` |
| any other | one | concentrated likelihood | each unit's intercept is solved for given slopes; small-T bias in the dispersion |

Poisson fixed effects are the usual first choice: the slopes are consistent
even when the counts are overdispersed or not Poisson at all, as long as
the mean is right, and the default cluster-robust standard errors account
for the overdispersion.

## 2. Site fixed effects

Here `washington_roads` has `r length(unique(washington_roads$ID))`
segments, most observed in three years. Traffic volume (`lnaadt`) changes
from year to year within a segment, but the speed indicator `speed50` does
not:

```{r fe}
fe <- countreg_fe(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + speed50 + offset(lnlength),
                  fixef = ~ ID, data = washington_roads)
summary(fe)
```

Two things happened before estimation, and both are reported:

* **Segments with no crashes in any year were dropped.** Their fixed effect
  would be $-\infty$; they carry no information on the slopes. So were
  segments observed only once.
* **`speed50` was removed.** A regressor that is constant within every unit
  is absorbed by the unit's fixed effect, so its coefficient is not
  identified. Time-invariant characteristics can only be studied with
  random-effects or pooled models.

```{r dropped}
length(fe$model$dropped$ID)     # segments dropped
fe$model$not_identified         # regressors removed
```

The standard errors are cluster-robust by segment (`stderr = "cluster"`,
the default). Other covariance matrices are available after the fit:

```{r vcov}
sqrt(diag(vcov(fe)))                      # clustered by segment
sqrt(diag(vcov(fe, type = "hessian")))    # Poisson model-based
```

The model-based standard error is much smaller: it assumes the Poisson
variance, which these counts exceed.

## 3. Site and year fixed effects

Crash counts often share year-to-year changes (weather, reporting, the
economy). A second fixed-effect dimension absorbs them:

```{r twoway}
fe2 <- countreg_fe(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + offset(lnlength),
                   fixef = ~ ID + Year, data = washington_roads)
summary(fe2)
fe2$model$fixef$fe2                       # year effects
```

With few levels, a dimension like `Year` can also enter the formula as a
factor; with several high-dimensional effects (sites and corridor-years,
say), the alternating projections keep the computation fast.

## 4. Comparison with pooled and random-effects models

The elasticity of crashes with respect to traffic volume from the pooled,
random-effects and fixed-effects Poisson models:

```{r compare}
f <- Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + offset(lnlength)
pooled <- countreg(f, data = washington_roads, family = "POISSON",
                   method = "BFGS", cluster = ~ ID)
re <- repois(f, data = washington_roads, group_var = "ID")
est <- function(m) c(estimate = coef(m)[["lnaadt"]],
                     se = sqrt(diag(vcov(m)))[["lnaadt"]])
round(rbind(pooled = est(pooled), random_effects = est(re),
            fixed_effects = est(fe2)), 3)
```

The pooled and random-effects estimates use the differences *between*
segments in traffic volume, which are large; the fixed-effects estimate
uses only the changes *within* segments over three years, which are small,
so its standard error is much larger. A big gap between the random-effects
and fixed-effects estimates suggests that the segment effects are related
to traffic volume, which would bias the random-effects estimate.

## 5. Other families

Any family of `countreg()` (and any family made with `new_count_family()`)
can be used with one fixed-effect dimension. The negative binomial (NB2)
fixed-effects model is the dummy-variable NB2, with the unit intercepts
concentrated out.

For the road segments, NB2 fixed effects reduce to the Poisson model: once
each segment has its own intercept, no overdispersion remains in three
years of counts, and the estimate of $\alpha$ goes to 0 (the fit warns that
the likelihood is flat in `ln(alpha)`). The Poisson fixed-effects model of
Section 2 is then the right one.

To show the NB2 model where it matters, simulate 300 units observed for 5
periods, with unit effects correlated with `x1` and overdispersed counts
(NB2 with $\alpha = 0.5$):

```{r nb2}
set.seed(11)
G <- 300; n_t <- 5
sim <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(G), each = n_t),
                  t = rep(seq_len(n_t), G))
a_i <- rnorm(G, 0, 0.7)
sim$x1 <- rnorm(nrow(sim)) + 0.5 * a_i[sim$id]
sim$x2 <- rnorm(nrow(sim))
sim$y <- rnbinom(nrow(sim), size = 2,
                 mu = exp(0.5 + a_i[sim$id] + 0.6 * sim$x1 - 0.4 * sim$x2))

fe_nb <- countreg_fe(y ~ x1 + x2, fixef = ~ id, data = sim, family = "NB2")
fe_nb_jk <- countreg_fe(y ~ x1 + x2, fixef = ~ id, data = sim,
                        family = "NB2", jackknife = TRUE, time = "t")
round(rbind(truth = c(0.6, -0.4, log(0.5)),
            NB2_FE = coef(fe_nb),
            jackknife = coef(fe_nb_jk)), 3)
```

The slopes are close to the truth, but the dispersion $\ln\alpha$ is
underestimated, because the fixed effects absorb much of the variation
between units. Two cautions apply to non-Poisson fixed effects in short
panels:

* The slopes have a small bias of order $1/T$ (Allison and Waterman 2002);
  the dispersion has a large one.
* `jackknife = TRUE` applies the split-panel jackknife of Dhaene and
  Jochmans (2015). In simulations like this one, with 200 units, it removed
  most of the dispersion bias with 5 or 10 periods but did not improve the
  slopes, and with 3 periods its half-panels are too short (a warning is
  given below 4 periods).

The Hausman, Hall and Griliches "conditional negative binomial" is a
different model, whose fixed effect enters the dispersion, not the mean; it
is not provided.

## 6. Correlated random effects: a test of random against fixed effects

Random-effects models can be kept, and the question of section 4 tested,
with the device of Mundlak (1978): add each unit's mean of the
time-varying regressors to the model. The random effect may then depend
on the regressors through their means, and the coefficient of the
regressor itself is a within-unit effect, as in the fixed-effects model.
`cre =` does this in `repois()`, `renb()` and `countreg_rp()`:

```{r cre}
cre <- repois(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + offset(lnlength), group_var = "ID",
              data = washington_roads, cre = ~ lnaadt, method = "BFGS",
              stderr = "robust")
round(coef(cre)[c("lnaadt", "mean_lnaadt")], 3)
cre_test(cre)
```

`cre_test()` is a Wald test that the coefficients of the means are zero.
With robust standard errors it is a robust version of the Hausman test
(Wooldridge 2019). A small p-value says that the segment effects are
related to traffic volume: the plain random-effects estimate of section 4
is then biased, and the within-segment effect (the coefficient of
`lnaadt` here, or the fixed-effects estimate) is the one to report.

In simulations with 300 units and 5 periods, when the unit effects were
correlated with the regressor the plain random-effects slope was biased
(0.63 for a true 0.5), while the model with `cre` gave 0.505, equal to the
fixed-effects estimate, and `cre_test()` rejected in every replication.
With uncorrelated effects all three were unbiased and the test rejected
in 7% of replications at the 5% level.

The group means are computed on the estimation rows and stored with the
fit, so predictions for a known unit use its training means: rows of
`newdata` never change them.

## 7. Predictions

Predictions for a known segment use its estimated fixed effect. A segment
that was not in the estimation data has no fixed effect, so its prediction
is `NA` unless you ask for the mean effect explicitly (the mean of the
estimated effects weighted by the segments' sizes in the estimation data,
fixed at estimation):

```{r predict}
nd <- washington_roads[washington_roads$ID %in%
                         names(fe2$model$fixef$fe1)[1:2], ]
predict(fe2, newdata = nd)

new_site <- nd[1, ]
new_site$ID <- "not-in-data"
predict(fe2, newdata = new_site)
predict(fe2, newdata = new_site, newgroup = "mean_fe")
```

## 8. Agreement with other software

The Poisson estimates, log-likelihoods and dropped groups equal those of
`fixest::fepois()`, and the NB2 estimates those of `fixest::fenegbin()`
and of `MASS::glm.nb()` with segment dummies. The cluster-robust standard
errors use the factor $G/(G-1)$ for $G$ clusters; they equal fixest's when
the clustering is given explicitly (`vcov = ~ ID`; fixest 0.13 and later
default to iid standard errors) with `ssc(adj = FALSE)`, as fixest by
default also multiplies the variance by $(n-1)/(n-K)$.

## References

Allison, P.D. and Waterman, R.P. (2002). Fixed-effects negative binomial
regression models. *Sociological Methodology*, 32, 247-265.

Dhaene, G. and Jochmans, K. (2015). Split-panel jackknife estimation of
fixed-effect models. *Review of Economic Studies*, 82(3), 991-1030.

Mundlak, Y. (1978). On the pooling of time series and cross section
data. *Econometrica*, 46(1), 69-85.

Wooldridge, J.M. (1999). Distribution-free estimation of some nonlinear
panel data models. *Journal of Econometrics*, 90(1), 77-97.

Wooldridge, J.M. (2019). Correlated random effects models with unbalanced
panels. *Journal of Econometrics*, 211(1), 137-150.
